subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: The probabilities of three mutually exclusive events are respectively given as (1 + 3p)/3, (1 − p)/4, (1 − 2p)/2. Prove that 1/3 ≤ p ≤ 1/2.

mark_split.label: Bounds on p from each of the three probabilities
Bound on p from the sum of the three (mutually exclusive)

No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper (no second Maths-2A source in the corpus; answer-book/papers/ holds first-year physics only) — recorded, not hidden. Answer checked: the four ranges are −1/3 ≤ p ≤ 2/3, −3 ≤ p ≤ 1, −1/2 ≤ p ≤ 1/2 and 1/3 ≤ p ≤ 13/3; the common part is 1/3 ≤ p ≤ 1/2 — agrees with the book. The sum simplifies as (4(1 + 3p) + 3(1 − p) + 6(1 − 2p))/12 = (13 − 3p)/12, which the book also has.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove the bounds on p — the fact about every probability, the three separate inequalities, the inequality from the sum, and how the four combine.
insider_note: The sum inequality is the only step that uses "mutually exclusive", and it is the step that gives the lower bound 1/3. The single-event bounds alone give only p ≤ 1/2.

steps.label: Each probability is in [0, 1]
steps.margin_note: First mark. State the rule and write the three inequalities it gives before solving any of them.

lines.text: The probability of any event lies between 0 and 1.

recall.must_convey: That every probability lies between 0 and 1, so each of the three given expressions is between 0 and 1.
accept: every probability is between zero and one so each of the three expressions is between zero and one
each given probability satisfies zero less than or equal to it less than or equal to one
write zero to one bounds for all three expressions
prathi probability zero and one madhya untundi, so moodu expressions ki aa bounds rayali
the three expressions each lie in the closed interval zero to one

steps.why: Nothing else is known about p. The only tools are that each expression is a probability, and that the three events cannot overlap.
common_mistakes: Using only the upper bound 1 and forgetting the lower bound 0.
Starting from the sum without the single-event bounds.

steps.label: Solve the three inequalities
steps.margin_note: Three marks, one per inequality. Multiply through by the denominator, then isolate p. When dividing by a negative number, reverse the inequality signs.

recall.must_convey: That solving the three inequalities gives −1/3 ≤ p ≤ 2/3, −3 ≤ p ≤ 1 and −1/2 ≤ p ≤ 1/2, reversing the signs when dividing by a negative.
accept: the first gives minus one third to two thirds the second minus three to one and the third minus half to half
solve each inequality for p reversing the sign when dividing by a negative
from the three expressions p is between minus a third and two thirds, minus three and one, minus half and half
moodu inequalities solve cheste minus one by three to two by three, minus three to one, minus half to half vasthai
each expression gives an interval for p, the tightest upper bound is half

steps.why: Each inequality on its own restricts p. The third gives p ≤ 1/2, the upper bound to be proved; the lower bound 1/3 is not among these three and must come from somewhere else.
common_mistakes: Not reversing the inequality signs when dividing by −1 or −2.
Multiplying only one side by the denominator.
Writing p ≤ 2/3 from (1) and then forgetting the lower bound from (1).

steps.label: Sum of the three probabilities ≤ 1
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Mutually exclusive events: the probability of their union is the SUM, and that union is an event, so the sum is between 0 and 1. Common denominator 12: 4(1 + 3p) + 3(1 − p) + 6(1 − 2p) = 13 − 3p.

lines.text: The three events are mutually exclusive, so the
probability of their union is the sum, which

recall.must_convey: That because the events are mutually exclusive the sum of the three probabilities is itself a probability, between 0 and 1, which gives 1/3 ≤ p ≤ 13/3.
accept: mutually exclusive so the sum of the three probabilities is between zero and one which gives one third less than or equal to p less than or equal to thirteen by three
add the three expressions over twelve to get thirteen minus three p over twelve between zero and one
the union probability is the sum and it is at most one so p is at least a third
mutually exclusive kabatti sum kuda probability, zero and one madhya, so p one by three nunchi thirteen by three
sum bound gives thirteen minus three p between zero and twelve

steps.why: This is the only step that uses "mutually exclusive", and it is the step that supplies the lower bound 1/3. Without it the proof cannot reach the stated range.
common_mistakes: Writing the sum = 1 (exhaustive) instead of ≤ 1 — the question does not say the events are exhaustive.
Combining the fractions wrongly: over 12 the numerators are 4, 3 and 6 times the brackets.
Losing the sign reversal when dividing −3p by −3.

steps.label: Intersect the four ranges
steps.margin_note: Last mark. p must satisfy all four. The largest lower bound is 1/3 (from (4)); the smallest upper bound is 1/2 (from (3)).

lines.text: Largest lower bound 1/3, smallest upper bound 1/2:

recall.must_convey: That taking the common part of the four ranges gives 1/3 ≤ p ≤ 1/2 — the largest lower bound and the smallest upper bound.
accept: take the common part of all four ranges, the largest lower bound is a third and the smallest upper bound is half
intersect the four intervals to get one third to one half
p must satisfy all four so it is between one by three and one by two
nalugu ranges common part teeste one by three to half vasthundi
the intersection of the intervals is a third to a half hence proved

steps.why: Each range is a condition p must meet; meeting all of them means lying in every range at once, which is their intersection.
common_mistakes: Taking the union of the ranges instead of the intersection.
Reporting the range from (4) alone, 1/3 ≤ p ≤ 13/3.
